Maintenance and future perspectives
text:
The problem of maintenance


Biology interpretation and data analysis depend on software




Many of the tools are developed by trainees, PhD students and postdocs




Funding encourages new applications, not maintenance




Circa one every four published tools becomes inaccesible




Therefore, maintenance must be planned as part of service delivery from the very beggining

title: Maintenance and future perspectives
text:
Security requirements @EMBL

Service needs to have a technical owner responsible for updating the service
Asset data needs to be classified according to its sensitivity
Service should be isolated and connections encrypted
In case of a Security incident, the technical owner must contact the Computer Security Incident Response Team and the Data Protection Office1

More info in the EMBL intranet

title: Information
text:
Description of the module
Public data services are an important part of the infrastructure supporting modern research, ranging from databases and data resources to software tools and other publicly accessible digital services.
This module introduces key considerations when planning, developing, providing, and maintaining public data services. Participants will explore the lifecycle of a service, from identifying user needs and assessing feasibility to choosing provision and release models, supporting users, monitoring service performance, and planning for long-term maintenance and sustainability.
Using examples from existing research data services, the module will also discuss organisational responsibilities, resourcing, scalability, security, legal considerations, and emerging developments such as AI-based interfaces and machine-to-machine access to services.

title: Information
text:
Prerequisites
No specific technical prerequisites are required.
Participants should have a general understanding of research data, software, or digital research infrastructure. Experience with developing, maintaining, supporting, or using research data services is beneficial but not required.
Participants are encouraged to bring an idea for an existing or potential public data service that they can use as a case throughout the module.

title: Information
text:
Learning outcomes
After this module the participants will be able to:

Identify and analyse user needs, organisational requirements, and available resources relevant to the provision of a public data service.
Plan appropriate approaches for user support, feedback, monitoring, scalability, and evaluation of a public data service.
Identify key considerations for the long-term maintenance and sustainability of a public data service, including dependencies, documentation, security, licensing, and data protection.
Evaluate how a public data service may need to evolve in response to changing user needs and technologies, and modes of access.

title: Material
text:
Discussion questions






WarningQuestion 1



You have a fantastic new idea for novel web platform but it’s hard to describe in words.
What mechanisms could you use to convey what the platform is meant to do?
Consider:

What is your use-case and how would you communicate it?
What is the minimum information deemed necessary to show its potential use?
An image is worth 1000 words









WarningQuestion 2



Your time with your present organisation is coming to an end.
Would you like your services to outlive your stay? What strategies can you use to ensure the service remains available?
Consider:

Financial or human resource needs.
Brand and relocating the service.
Changing needs and service sunsetting.









WarningQuestion 3



Imagine your service has existed for three years.
How would you convince a funder that it has been successful?
Consider:

What evidence would you collect?
Which KPIs would you track?
What stories would you tell?









WarningQuestion 4



The ecosystem where your service is provided changed impacting it (positively or negatively).
How would you assess this impact and what measures could you implement to adapt?
Consider:

Resourcing necessary.
Synergies with other existing services.
Building on brand, reputation or merit for continuation and sustainability.









WarningQuestion 5



Imagine a user encounters a problem with your service, either a bug in the system or they just want user guidance.
How should they contact you?
Discuss:

Which reporting channels would you offer?
Which channel would you recommend as the primary route?
How would you ensure reports are not lost?









WarningQuestion 6



You want to introduce a major new feature.
How would you test it before releasing it broadly?
Would you use:

Prototypes
Pilot users
Proof-of-concepts
A/B testing

What are the advantages and disadvantages of your chosen approach?








WarningQuestion 7



You ask your favourite AI assistant to edit a Python script of your data service to make it faster.
How would you assure it still performs as expected?

What are the advantages and disadvantages of your chosen approach?









WarningQuestion 8



Have you tried to use a published software data service and it did not work?
Discuss:

What was the reason?
What was the maintenance issue?
How could it have been avoided?

Which one to choose?

Depends on the user interaction:
Technical users -> GitHub Issues
General users -> support email or form
